title: Four readings of Swedish inflation explain Thedéen’s case to parliament
summary: At the Riksdag Finance Committee on 19 November, Governor Erik Thedéen faced a straightforward question. Sweden’s CPIF inflation had just fallen to 1.1%. Why had the Riksbank delivered its first interest-rate increase in three years, taking the policy rate to 2%? His answer turned on what prices included, when the forces affecting them would fade and how quickly monetary policy could influence demand. His opening remarks described a reduction in the support afforded by rates as growth strengthened. The accompanying presentation supplies the figures needed to judge that argument (published remarks and slides 4–8).

October CPIF inflation was 1.1%, down from 1.5% in September. Excluding energy, it fell from 0.5% to 0.1%. But a separate calculation that removed the direct price effects of temporary fiscal measures put the October figure at 2.5%, down from 3.0%. Excluding both energy and those fiscal effects produced yet another result, 1.1% after 1.6%. The fiscal adjustment covers temporary tax reductions on food and fuel and lower public transport fares. In both months these measures held headline inflation well below the adjusted figure. Energy, meanwhile, pushed in the opposite direction. No single exclusion captures all the relevant pressures. All four rates nevertheless fell between September and October, an important qualification to a policy case based on what inflation would do next (slide 8, outcomes table and footnote).

The external shocks did not all point in the same direction for growth. The presentation associated the Middle East war with weaker output and more expensive energy, while the AI investment expansion supported output and equity valuations and increased demand for inputs such as semiconductors. Both could lift inflation and interest rates. Freight costs differed by vessel type, and futures suggested a decline in oil prices from elevated levels. The chart distinguishes observed prices from futures and averages daily contracts over five days for the curves shown at each monetary policy meeting. Treating the downward-sloping part of the chart as an observed decline in energy costs would remove a central uncertainty from the analysis (slides 2–3).

Domestic evidence helped explain why the Riksbank had waited while other central banks raised rates and why the case for waiting had weakened. Growth and inflation had previously been more subdued in Sweden. By the hearing, business confidence was stronger than usual across a range of sectors. The sentiment measures summarised order books, production, hiring plans and sales. The household series was visibly weaker than the business measure. Employment and unemployment charts distinguished the newly observed third-quarter figures from the forecast improvement in labour-market conditions. The increase in producer costs also extended beyond energy: the domestic supply price index shown on slide 7 excludes energy and covers goods sold in Sweden. Price pressure in that measure is consistent with broader upstream costs, although it does not identify how much will pass into final consumer prices (slides 5–7).

The Governor also addressed rate comparisons across countries. Forward-looking policy implied that the Swedish rate path could gradually normalise as the recovery progressed. The international comparison distinguished observed daily policy rates, a projected Swedish quarterly average and an estimated range for the longer-run neutral rate. These are different objects with different degrees of uncertainty. The final market exhibit showed increases in ten-year government bond yields since 31 December 2025 across Sweden, Germany, Britain, the United States and France. Sweden had the smallest increase of the five, France the largest. The Governor listed several possible drivers, including stronger growth, inflation expectations, fiscal risks and debt-financed AI investment. A year-to-date change cannot measure the market response to the November Swedish rate decision or isolate the contribution of any one of those influences (slides 4, 9–10 and fiscal appendix, slide 12).

The hearing therefore provided more than a restatement of the rate decision. It put numbers on how temporary fiscal relief and energy affected the reading of headline inflation, while evidence on demand and producer prices addressed the risk beyond those temporary effects. The Governor continued to describe the longer-term rate path as conditional on new information. His account did not promise another move on a particular date, and his market charts did not estimate the yield or currency impact of parliamentary testimony (closing remarks).

questions.question: Which measure best predicted inflation after the temporary fiscal measures expired?
questions.detail: Track CPIF, CPIF excluding energy, the fiscal-adjusted series and its energy-excluded counterpart from the same data vintage. Compare components as tax and fare changes drop out of annual rates. Keep that arithmetic effect distinct from firms increasing underlying selling prices.

questions.question: Was the recovery strong enough for non-energy input costs to pass through?
questions.detail: Compare the domestic supply price index with realised consumer prices in matched categories, and relate the gap to household demand and business sentiment. Look for persistence across categories as well as the headline rate. The slide deck documents the pressure on producers, while this test addresses its next stage.

questions.question: Which parts of the yield change were global and which were specific to Swedish policy?
questions.detail: Measure Swedish yields relative to comparable maturities abroad around identifiable domestic announcements. Use the year-to-date comparison only as background, and control for international energy, fiscal and technology news. Comparing the hearing window with the earlier rate-decision window would separate two different information events.
